title: Ἁλκύων
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 28. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἁλκύων ὄρνεόν ἐστι φιλέρημον διὰ παντὸς ἐν θαλάττῃ διαιτώμενον.
sentences.tr: Halkyōn orneon esti philerēmon dia pantos en thalattēi diaitōmenon.
sentences.l: The halcyon is a bird fond-of-solitude, through all time on the sea passing its life.
sentences.i: The halcyon is a bird that loves solitude and lives its whole life at sea.
sentences.n: The ἁλκυών is the kingfisher, and the ancients held that it nested on the sea itself during a stretch of windless winter weather — our 'halcyon days'. διὰ παντός, 'through everything', is the ordinary idiom for 'continually'; χρόνου is understood. φιλέρημον is φίλος + ἔρημος, 'friend of the lonely place'. Chambry prints the name with a rough breathing, Ἁλκύων — hence the h- in the romanization; the lexica head the word with the smooth ἀλκυών, and the breathing was unsettled in antiquity, some hearing ἅλς, 'sea', inside the name.

sentences.t: Ταύτην λέγεται τὰς τῶν ἀνθρώπων θήρας φυλαττομένην ἐν σκοπέλοις παραθαλαττίοις νεοττοποιεῖσθαι.
sentences.tr: Tautēn legetai tas tōn anthrōpōn thēras phylattomenēn en skopelois parathalattiois neottopoieisthai.
sentences.l: Her it is said, guarding-against the huntings of men, to nest on crags beside the sea.
sentences.i: She is said to keep clear of men's hunting and to build her nest on the sea-cliffs.
sentences.n: λέγεται used impersonally, 'it is said', with an accusative-and-infinitive hanging on it (Ταύτην … νεοττοποιεῖσθαι) — the accusative comes first, long before its infinitive. φυλάττομαι in the middle takes an accusative of what one is on guard against; that verb is the hinge of the whole fable and returns twice more. νεοττοποιεῖσθαι is νεοττός 'chick' + ποιέω, 'to make chicks', i.e. to nest.

sentences.t: Καὶ δή ποτε τίκτειν μέλλουσα παρεγένετο εἴς τι ἀκρωτήριον καὶ θεασαμένη πέτραν ἐπὶ θαλάττῃ ἐνταῦθα ἐνεοττοποιεῖτο.
sentences.tr: Kai dē pote tiktein mellousa paregeneto eis ti akrōtērion kai theasamenē petran epi thalattēi entautha eneottopoieito.
sentences.l: And so once, being-about to lay, she came to a certain headland and, having beheld a rock upon the sea, there she was nesting.
sentences.i: One day, when she was about to lay, she came to a headland, and seeing a rock at the sea's edge she made her nest there.
sentences.n: Καὶ δή ποτε is the storyteller's 'and then one day' — it turns the standing description into a single event. μέλλω + infinitive for what is on the point of happening. ἐπὶ θαλάττῃ with the dative is place, 'on/at the sea', not motion.

sentences.t: Ἐξελθούσης δὲ αὐτῆς ποτε ἐπὶ νομήν, συνέβη τὴν θάλασσαν ὑπὸ λαβροῦ πνεύματος κυματωθεῖσαν ἐξαρθῆναι μέχρι τῆς καλιᾶς καὶ ταύτην ἐπικλύσασαν τοὺς νεοττοὺς διαφθεῖραι.
sentences.tr: Exelthousēs de autēs pote epi nomēn, synebē tēn thalassan hypo labrou pneumatos kymatōtheisan exarthēnai mechri tēs kalias kai tautēn epiklysasan tous neottous diaphtheirai.
sentences.l: But she having gone out once after food, it came about that the sea, having been raised into waves by a violent wind, was lifted as far as the nest, and that, having flooded over this, it destroyed the nestlings.
sentences.i: One day, while she was out foraging, a violent wind raised the sea into waves that rose as far as the nest; the water washed over the nest and destroyed the chicks.
sentences.n: Ἐξελθούσης … αὐτῆς is a genitive absolute: a participle and its own subject standing loose from the main clause, the standard Greek way of saying 'while she was out'. You will meet it in nearly every fable. συνέβη, 'it came about', then governs two infinitives (ἐξαρθῆναι, διαφθεῖραι) with τὴν θάλασσαν as their subject; ταύτην is the nest, the object of ἐπικλύσασαν. Note that Chambry prints θάλασσαν here beside θαλάττῃ in the first line — the Attic -ττ- and the common -σσ- forms stand side by side in the text as transmitted.

sentences.t: Καὶ ἡ ἁλκύων ἐπανελθοῦσα, ὡς ἔγνω τὸ γεγονός, εἶπεν· « Ἀλλ’ ἔγωγε δειλαία, ἥτις τὴν γῆν ὡς ἐπίβουλον φυλαττομένη, ἐπὶ ταύτην κατέφυγον, ἣ πολλῷ μοι γέγονεν ἀπιστοτέρα. »
sentences.tr: Kai hē halkyōn epanelthousa, hōs egnō to gegonos, eipen· « All’ egōge deilaia, hētis tēn gēn hōs epiboulon phylattomenē, epi tautēn katephygon, hē pollōi moi gegonen apistotera. »
sentences.l: And the halcyon, having come back, when she learned what had happened, said: « Ah, wretched I, who, guarding-against the land as treacherous, fled for refuge to this one — which has proved by much more untrustworthy to me. »
sentences.i: The halcyon came back, and when she saw what had happened she said, « Wretched creature that I am: I was on my guard against the land as a plotter, and took refuge with the sea, which has proved far less to be trusted. »
sentences.n: ἥτις, the indefinite relative, carries a shade of cause — 'I, seeing that I…' — and explains the self-reproach. τὸ γεγονός is a perfect participle used as a noun, 'the thing that has come to pass'. πολλῷ is the dative of degree of difference beside a comparative, 'by much'. ἀπιστοτέρα is 'less to be trusted' rather than 'more unbelieving'.

sentences.t: Οὕτω καὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἔνιοι τοὺς ἐχθροὺς φυλαττόμενοι λανθάνουσιν πολλῷ χαλεπωτέροις τῶν ἐχθρῶν φίλοις ἐμπίπτοντες.
sentences.tr: Houtō kai tōn anthrōpōn enioi tous echthrous phylattomenoi lanthanousin pollōi chalepōterois tōn echthrōn philois empiptontes.
sentences.l: So too some of men, guarding-against their enemies, escape their own notice falling in with friends by much harsher than their enemies.
sentences.i: So too some men, on their guard against enemies, fall unawares among friends far harsher than any enemy.
sentences.n: λανθάνουσιν … ἐμπίπτοντες: λανθάνω with a participle, one of the neatest Greek idioms — 'they escape notice falling in with', that is, they fall in with them without realising it. The moral repeats the story's two key words, φυλάττομαι and πολλῷ, so that the halcyon's mistake and the human one are shown to be one and the same. τῶν ἐχθρῶν after the comparative is the genitive of comparison, 'than their enemies'.
